label: paragraph_title
text: SOMERSET MAUGHAM

label: text
text: "PAINTED VEIL" AUTHOR IN HONGKONG.

label: text
text: "UNNECESSARY FUSS."

label: text
text: His Characters As "Purely Imaginary"

label: text
text: The coldest man in Hongkong today is probably Mr. Somerset Maugham, playwright, novelist and traveller, best known in Hongkong as author of "The Painted Vell", a book which was given much free advertisement owing to the holding up of the first edition and the changing of the scenes from Hongkong to an imaginary place.

label: text
text: Mr. Maugham was to catch a boat at Manila to take him direct to Saigon but he missed it and has come to Hongkong in order to make a connection with the U.S. "Hanoi" which leaves to-morrow. He is collecting material for a volume of short stories about Malaya. Borneo and the Far East.

label: text
text: Having undertaken the trip from Manila to Hongkong at a moment's notice through force of circumstances, Mr. Naugham has only his summer clothes and a topee with him. "You find me rather chilly," he remarked to a "China Mail" representative who interviewed him this morning.

label: text
text: Asked if Hongkong would figure in these stories, Mr Maugham shook his head. A novelist was always on the look out for subject matter, however, he added, and something might strike him as worth noting here. With regard to "The Fainted Veil," a subject which the "China Mail" representative introduced, Mr. Maugham said that a lot of unnecessary fuss had been made. The plot and characters were purely imaginary.

label: text
text:
As to the general manner of his approach of subjects and places for his books and descriptions, Mr. Maugham said that he always made it a practice to become acquainted with places before he wrote about them. His stories were not intended to apply to personalities literally. Experiences he heard of in different places might provide an idea but real life was never complete enough for a satisfactory story to be made of it.
“In all stories it might be said that perhaps fifteen per cent. is life and the rest invention,” added Mr. Maugham. “Any sensible novelist who wanted to put scenes into his story, however, should stop long enough to get acquainted with such details as he wanted to use. “I find a certain interest in studying exotic surroundings and customs and the effect on the characters of the white people who live among them.”

label: paragraph_title
text: A Novelist's Aims

label: text
text: Asked if he found it easy to write now that he had a considerable number of books and plays to his name, Mr. Maugham said that he never ceased to find it difficult to write. "There is a great gulf between having an idea of what you want to say in your own mind and getting it down on paper. I am never entirely satisfied at what I would like to write and what I find I can. English is a difficult language in which to couch expression. Hardly anyone has realized perfect expression in it."

label: text
text: In conclusion, the newspaper man asked Mr. Maugham if he had any self imposed ideal before him in his writings. "I try to instruct, educate or moralise to no-one," said the novelist. "I try to move, to interest and to amuse. That, I think, should be the aim of the novelist."

label: text
text: Prior to coming to the Far East, a London critic wrote of Mr. Maugham as follows: "The man never stays still. When you think the time is ripe for him triumphantly to tour America—when "The Moon and Sixpence" has attracted the widest attention—he insists on going immediately to China. This may be because, though well set up black-eyed, broad-framed, and excessively handsome in evening clothes, he is rather difficult."

label: text
text: Writing of Mr. Somerset Maugham's book "On A Chinese Screen!" a reviewer stated: Just as a picture may be composed of a number of coloured patches juxtaposed and sometimes superimposed upon one another, each colour being applied upon its own particular block so Mr. Somerset Maugham has produced an impression of China by means of fifty-eight brief glimpses at a great variety of things seen there. Some of the assays—and their contribution to the total impression is as large as the rest—tell of Europeans encountered in China.

label: text
text: HAWKERS' LUCK.

label: text
text: With the relaxation in the law against unlicensed hawkers and the general falling off in crime, there were few cases in the Police Courts this morning.

label: text
text: Forbidden Newspapers:

label: text
text: An employee of the "Tai Kwong Po" newspaper was charged before Mr. R. E. Lindsell with the possession of 21 different newspapers published in Canton, the circulation of which is forbidden in the Colony. Defendant was arrested as he was leaving the wharf after boarding the S.S. "Lungshan" which arrived from Canton on Tuesday afternoon.

label: text
text: Detective-Sub-Inspector Shannon explained the delay in bringing the defendant before His Worship by stating that he had to submit the newspapers to the Secretary for Chinese Affairs to have translations taken.

label: text
text: Defendant said that he was only carrying out the instructions of his master to receive the newspapers from a man on board. His Worship agreed there was some truth in this story, and remained defendant on $200 bail until Monday, pending enquiries as to why the "Tai Kwong Po" imported the papers.

label: text
text: A Chinese youngster was charged before Major C. Willson with the theft of $20 from Mr. H. Pritham, of On-Hing Terrace.

label: text
text: Defendant said that he found the money on the ground while doing some odd jobs in complainant's house and he placed the notes inside his shoe.

label: text
text: The Magistrate imposed sentence of three weeks' hard labour and eight strokes of the birch.

label: text
text: On a charge of unlawful possession of a quantity of cloth,g and an electric fan, two Chinese explained that the articles were given to them in lieu of wages by the master of a Chinese firm which had closed down. This was later borne out by the wife of the man.

label: text
text: Sergeant Brittain said that the master was the debtor in a bank-ruptcy case at the Summary Court yesterday, who is believed to have absconded.

label: text
text: The Magistrate said he did not wish to imprisonment on account of his youth, and ordered him to sign a bond for good behaviour in a sum of $250.

label: text
text: C. T. French, wireless watchman of the s.s. "Delta," was again before the Kowloon Magistrate this morning to receive sentence in a charge of theft of passengers' belongings which was proved against him on Wednesday.

label: text
text: Defendants were discharged.

text: At an investiture at Buckingham Palace His Majesty the King bestowed the Board of Trade silver medal for rescue work during a typhoon in Hongkong harbour to Messrs. George Parker, John Smight, and Harold Wainwright, ex-apprentices on the 5.8. "Egremont Castle."

label: paragraph_title

label: paragraph_title
text: Work of “Egremont Castle.”

label: paragraph_title
text: 一当

label: text
text: The foregoing refers to the disastrous typhoon of August 18, 1923, which resulted in the loss of the Indo-China s.s. "Loong Sang," which, founded with loss of many lives after being swept away from her mooring. One of the British submarines—the L9—went down near Queen's Pier, the crew being saved by the Japanese steamer "Ginyo Maru." The liners "Empress of Australia" and "Andre Lebon" were in great danger for a time owing to their anchors dragging.

label: text
text: The officers and crew of the 5.s. "Egremont Castle," which was dragging her anchors near Stonecutter's Island, performed fine heroic work, saving the cook-boy of the 5.s. "Loong Sang" and other persons from vessels drifting down stream.

label: text
text: His Majesty the King cabled a message of sympathy to the Governor in regard to the sad loss of life and the damage to ships and property.

label: text
text: (Hculer'a Seroae.)

label: text
text: London Feb. 4

label: text
text: In the House of Commons, the debate on the Labour amendent to the Address in Reply to the Speech from The Throne, which was moved by Mr. R. Snowden, resolved itself into a discussion on Socialism versus non-Socialism.

label: text
text: Mr. Snowden contended that during the Government's year of office unemployment had increased wages had declined, and profits had risen.

label: text
text:
The Labourite, Mr. Johnston, referring to the projected Labour Hours Conference feared that the Washington Convention itself was destroyed by the Conference excluding India, China, and Japan; he emphasised the long hours and inferior conditions in Japan.
Sir John Simon (Liberal), in opposing the amendment, asked how the coal industry find makets under public control which was lacking under private ownership? Sir A. Steel-Maitland, replying, denied that the situation had become worse. Notably there had been an increase in wages, whilst as regards unemployment the Government would welcome the co-operation of all Parties, and was even willing to discuss the establishment of a joint Committee of all Parties.

label: text
text: The debate was adjourned.

label: paragraph_title

label: text
text: THOSE NEGOTIATIONS WITH AMOY

label: text
text: TERMS REJECTED.

label: text
text: At the time of a boom in shares of the Hongkong Electric Co., Ltd., about a year or so ago, a rumour was current that the company would benefit considerably by a concession in the foreign settlement of Kulangsu, Amoy.

label: text
text: Light. is now thrown on the matter by the “China Mail’s correspondent who reports the annual meeting of ratepayers.

label: paragraph_title
text: TENDERS STILL WANTED.

label: text
text: (From Our Own Correspondent.)

label: text
text:
For many months the question of ways and means of providing better electric light in the Settlement has been at issue. Reporting upon the matter, the Chairman of the Council said: "The electric light supply has, if anything, deteriorated and residents have to depend to a great extent on other means of lighting."
“In the meantime the efforts taken to obtain an improved service have proved abortive, but it is imperative that definite and decisive action be taken without further loss of time. The resolution unanimously adopted by the ratepayers at a special meeting held on September 19, 1924, authorising the Council to take steps to terminate the existing agreement, and to proceed to open negotiations with the Hongkong Electric Co., Ltd., resulted in a draft agreement being drawn up. This agreement was submitted to the ratepayers at a special meeting held on July 31, 1925, but was rejected. A committee of the Council is making investigations as to the most suitable method of solving the electric light question.”

label: text
text: After considerable discussion at the annual meeting on January 29, the following resolution was passed:

label: text
text: "Resolved: That the incoming Council call for tenders for the erection of an electric light and power plant on Kulangsu, and ask for particulars as to alternating current or direct current, or other similar terms, as they may decide, and submit said tenders to the ratepayers as soon as possible."

label: text
text: HOW OUR DONATION HELPED THE ADMIRALTY.

label: text
text: NAVAL POLICY REVIEWED

label: text
text: (British Wireless Service.)

label: text
text: Rugby Feb. 4.

label: text
text: Mr. W. C. Bridgeman, First Lord of the Admiralty, spoke in defence of the Government's naval policy at the Constitutional Club.

label: text
text: He expressed satisfaction that the Admiralty had been able to secure from the Government a programme, of reconstruction covering a period of years for the replacement of those ships that had become obsolete or were becoming obsolete. The value of that decision, he said, was very important.

label: text
text: Dependence on Trade.

label: text
text: The Washington Agreement on the dimensions of the Navies of the world had been faithfully observed by this country as by other countries. We were, however, not in exactly the same position as other countries, because we were no longer an island Power, and because we had an enormous expanse of Empire trade to be protected, on which this country depended for its very existence. We more than any other country depended upon cruisers to protect our trade.

label: text
text: The Washington Agreement laid down that the size of new cruisers should not exceed 10,000 tons and the armaments should not exceed eight-inch guns. Consequently, it was essential that our cruisers should be up to date, and that we should in their construction include those improvements which the lessons of the war had taught us.

label: text
text: OBSOLETE SHIPS USELESS.

label: text
text: It was no use going to sea against an enemy with obsolete ships. It would be a deception against the British public to tell them that we could rely upon old ships that had been knocked about in the war. Those old ships could no longer hold their own with the vessels laid down by other countries. If we were going to have total disarmament that would be another matter; but so long as other countries kept up a modern official Navy, so long was it still more essential for us to do the same.

label: text
text: Mr. Bridgeman added that we had been nobly supported by the Commonwealth of Australia. The contribution of a quarter of a million sterling from Hongkong had enabled the Admiralty to make a start with a floating dock in the Straits Settlements, which would at least provide for the docking of our capital ships.

label: text
text: As the Government proceeded, and as he hoped they would proceed with the full programme which was laid down for a complete base at Singapore, they would be ensuring not only the capacity of the British Fleet to defend British trade in those waters, but adding to its efficiency and economy.

label: text
text:
APPEAL FOR MORE HELP.
He would be glad to get further help from other parts of the Empire, and so, he thought, would the taxpayers of this country.

label: paragraph_title
text: PEACE TIME NEEDS.

label: text
text: (Reuter's Service.)

label: text
text:
Mr. W. C. Bridgeman, in the course of his speech at the Constitutional Club, said that the Navy must not be neglected even in peace time.
He thought that the Government was right and that Australia was right in pushing with the construction of up to date cruisers because we were getting very far behind. We were not leading in the race for competition with other naval Powers who began long before Britain but anyhow it was very satisfactory to know that Britain had got a programme laid down covering a number of years which would eventually produce a fleet of the most up-to-date cruisers possible.
